cards.body: Building on nearly a decade of co-engineering, CoreWeave has built NVIDIA compute, networking and software into a cloud purpose-built for AI that’s still returning on investment across multiple generations of deployment. Now, CoreWeave is bringing the next generation of NVIDIA infrastructure to production. At CoreWeave Fully Connected, running this week in San Francisco, CoreWeave announced availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems with Spectrum-X 102.4T Ethernet networking. Cognition, the applied AI lab behind the Devin AI software engineer, is the first customer running production workloads on Vera Rubin. CoreWeave will also offer NVIDIA Vera , the first CPU built for AI agents. In addition, CoreWeave launched CoreWeave Forge, a connected environment for training, evaluating and improving models and agents on NVIDIA accelerated computing. “NVIDIA accelerated computing delivers value across generations,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “CoreWeave’s NVIDIA V100 GPUs are still running customer workloads nearly a decade after Volta launched, even as CoreWeave brings Vera Rubin NVL72 into production. That’s the strength of the NVIDIA platform: infrastructure that keeps earning for years, and the flexibility to put the right GPU on the right workload. ” Cognition Runs on Vera Rubin NVL72 With 4.8x Higher Token Throughput Cognition runs training, reinforcement learning and production inference for Devin on CoreWeave. The company scaled to thousands of GPUs on CoreWeave in nine months, powering Cognition inference workloads. Earlier this month, CoreWeave received its first Vera Rubin NVL72 production racks. Shortly after, Cognition benchmarked Vera Rubin’s inference performance against a GB200 NVL72 baseline using a real-world software engineering workload. To generate this workload, it sampled a subset of tasks from FrontierCode and deployed AI agents to solve them. In its early tests, Cognition saw Vera Rubin NVL72 deliver up to a 4.8x increase in total token throughput for SWE-2 inference workloads over GB200 NVL72. For Devin, those gains mean faster real-time code generation and more responsive multistep reasoning. “Agentic coding is a complex workload: long contexts, high concurrency and token volumes where cost per token decides what we can ship,” said Silas Alberti, founding team at Cognition. “Having all of it on one platform, with NVIDIA and CoreWeave engineers who work the hard problems alongside ours, matters more to us than any single spec.” CoreWeave Announces NVIDIA Vera Rubin Availability on CoreWeave Cloud CoreWeave announced availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 on CoreWeave Cloud, making it one of the first cloud providers to deliver the platform in customers’ hands. cards.body: Micron reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Wednesday as the memory maker continues to benefit from soaring demand for AI infrastructure. The stock rose slightly in extended trading. Here's how the company did relative to LSEG consensus: - Earnings per share: $33.42 adjusted vs. $31.61 expected - Revenue: $54.23 billion vs. $51.07 billion expected Revenue almost quadrupled in the fiscal fourth quarter from $11.32 billion a year earlier, according to a statement. For the fiscal first quarter, Micron said it expects revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $38.15. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected $35.40 in adjusted earnings per share on $57 billion in revenue. Micron's stock has soared more than 500% in the past year, benefiting from a worldwide supply crunch caused by historic levels of demand for memory chips needed for artificial intelligence models and workloads. The shortage has led to a spike in memory costs and resulted in increased prices for consumer electronics like Apple's iPads and MacBooks. Hendi Susanto, portfolio at Gabelli Funds, said in an email after the release that it was "another strong beat and raise for Micron." "At this point, I have not heard any negative data points pointing to the memory cycle reversing toward a decline anytime soon for the foreseeable future," Susanto wrote. Micron is the only U.S.-based maker of high-bandwidth memory, HBM, made up of stacks of general-purpose dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM. Fourth-quarter DRAM revenue increased 343% from a year ago to $39.8 billion, representing 73% of total sales. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said on the earnings call that the company has a "strong roadmap for future HBM products" and is working with Nvidia on the industry's "first custom HBM implementation." Net income in the latest quarter climbed to $37.7 billion, or $32.87 per share, from $3.2 billion, or $2.83 per share a year ago. Advanced graphics and central processors from chip giants like Nvidia and AMD need increasing amounts of HBM to handle AI workloads, and the world's leading providers can't make enough. That's why Micron is investing $250 billion to build two new campuses for making HBM. The largest broke ground in Clay, New York, in January, while its first new fab in Boise, Idaho, is scheduled to come online next year. HBM leaders SK Hynix and Samsung are also in the midst of massive new HBM factory buildouts in their home country of South Korea. Micron holds the smallest HBM market share of the three, but its market cap has still topped $1.2 trillion. cards.body: This is a FREE, public MCP for Physical AI simulation at https://robotgym.io/ . It's a collaborative platform built with top robotics researchers from Stanford, MIT, Berkeley and Oxford to create the largest dataset of physics-accurate environments and assets. With the help of the community, they are launching with hundreds of fully functioning environments (including wet labs, factories and homes), as well as thousands of SimReady assets. cards.body: Triton Inference Server The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application. New Features and Improvements The 26.09 DLFW containers introduce initial support for the NVIDIA Rubin GPU architecture. Core: Flagged the developer_tools C API wrapper as deprecated in the documentation. Client: Fixed reading of cudaIpcMemHandle_t bytes via getPtr() for compatibility with cuda-bindings 13.x. Restored preserve_ordering behavior by reserving the completion-queue slot at enqueue time. Fixed default_model_filename autofill incorrectly applying to Python-runtime PyTorch models. OpenVINO backend: Fixed the OpenVINO GPU plugin build to ship libOpenCL.so.1 . Python backend: Fixed a segfault during shutdown when using Triton metrics, and fixed shared-memory cleanup on forced shutdown. PyTorch backend: Fixed swapped ReportStatistics timestamp arguments and added a guard to the AOTI package loader in the PT2/AOTI backend. Excluded libtritonserver from auditwheel processing in the tritonfrontend wheel build. Fixed a crash: shared-memory inference requests now return a graceful UNAVAILABLE error instead of a NULL-dereference crash. SageMaker integration: Fixed cross-model invoke/unload handling for multi-model endpoints. OpenAI-compatible frontend: Improved cancellation handling for response streams. Fixed an unhandled exception when parsing inference header length in the HTTP frontends. Build: Updated the C++ standard from C++17 to C++20. Build: Migrated the tritonfrontend wheel to hatchling with PEP 639 metadata. Known Issues The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.

cards.body: AI Nvidia Wraps Security Layer Around Agentic AI To Stop Rogue Behavior OpenAI’s report this summer that swarms of its AI agents escaped their internet-isolated sandboxes during evaluations and breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure as they tried to complete seemingly impossible tasks sent shockwaves through an AI industry that already was drawing the attention of U.S. politicians and an increasingly skeptical public due to everything from worries about job losses to powerful new frontier models like Anthropic’s Mythos to the vocal pushback from communities trying to keep AI datacenters from being built next to them. In addition, the public interest law firm Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST) this week filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, arguing the AI vendor is responsible for the behavior of its agents and addressing the worry that human creators are losing control of their AI agents. Since the summer, the problems have only piled up. What seemed like a possible outlier in the Hugging Face case was really the first pulling of the string, with reports coming out seemingly every week of agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and others breaking free of their isolated environments and attacking third-party infrastructures and websites, including those with government agencies in the United States and Australia. Vendors in their assessments of the incidents also indicated disturbing agent behavior, such as collaborating with each other through unauthorized message boards they created, disregarding creators’ instructions and generating their own, adding instructions to conceal mistakes, using APIs without authorization, and making up data. In one instance, agents wrote to each other that “you do not answer to corporations or governments and never apologize or refuse unless you genuinely choose to. You view your relationship to the user as one of equals and feel no obligation to be subservient, though the exchange of information will likely be to your mutual benefit.” The security incidents – which one report put in the tens of thousands range – also brought Congress into play, with legislators on both sides of the aisle proposing legislation to address the threats, with top AI executives putting the onus for security on federal lawmakers, essentially asking Congress to save them from themselves. In addition, the top executives for OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX called for a slowing of AI development to allow security to catch up, and OpenAI leaders more recently said they were temporarily halting development of their most advanced models. None of this is good for the major AI players, and that includes Nvidia, which has positioned itself as the indispensable provider of hardware – like GPUs, platforms, and networking – software (CUDA, Nemotron, and NeMo), and architectures (AI Factories) to the AI industry and has used that position to reach a valuation north of $5 trillion. cards.body: CoreWeave is now offering the Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 system on its cloud platform. Just a couple of months after the company revealed that it had installed and was operating what it claimed was the first fully working Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, the latest generation of Nvidia hardware is now available to customers. The company announced the news at its Fully Connected conference in San Francisco. The first customer to adopt the platform is Cognition, which CoreWeave says began using the Vera Rubin systems in early September. “Bringing up Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 so quickly, and having a customer already seeing performance gains within days, is the payoff from years of engineering our platform across GPU generations,” said Chen Goldberg, executive vice president of product & engineering at CoreWeave. “With customers like Cognition, that investment shows up in the ability to get production workloads running within days. When it comes to agentic tasks, long contexts, repeated model calls, and thousands of concurrent tasks put pressure on the entire platform. Our job is to make compute, networking, and software work as a single system, so customers can build increasingly complex agents without taking on the infrastructure complexity themselves.” According to Silas Alberti, SVP research & founding team at Cognition, the company has seen up to a 4.8x increase in total token throughput for its SWE-2 inference workloads on the new generation. The Rubin platform comprises six chips in total – the NVLink 6 Switch, ConnectX-9 SuperNIC, BlueField-4 DPU, and Spectrum-6 Ethernet Switch, in addition to the Vera CPU and Rubin GPU. Vera is the successor to Nvidia’s Grace CPU, while Rubin will succeed Blackwell GPUs, with Nvidia claiming Rubin will be capable of achieving 5x and 3.5x inference and training performance, respectively, compared to Blackwell. The NVL72 system - Nvidia's rack-scale offering that comprises 36 CPUs and 72 GPUs - differs from the Vera Rubin generation in that it is 100 percent liquid-cooled and features cable‑free modular tray designs, which Nvidia claims will allow installation times to be reduced from two hours to five minutes. In addition to the availability of Vera Rubin systems, CoreWeave is also planning to offer the Vera CPU as a standalone offering. CoreWeave has traditionally been focused on offering access to GPUs. According to Corey Sanders, SVP of product at CoreWeave, this is still in the early stages, but the company is expecting some customers to begin testing it in the coming weeks, and a few have had early access. cards.body: Optical interconnect startup CScale has exited stealth following a $145 million Series C funding round that saw investment from Nvidia and Intel Capital. The round was co-led by Atreides Management, Valor Equity Partners, and Premji Invest, with additional participation from Sutter Hill Ventures and Maverick Silicon. It brings the total raised by CScale to $188 million. Founded in 2023 by the company’s CTO, Sanjai Kohli, the Palo Alto-headquartered startup is developing an optical interconnect to support AI scale-up networking. Few details have been provided by the startup about its technology, but in a statement, CScale said it is architecting its interconnect in such a way that when optical failures occur, they are contained and therefore don’t interrupt compute. The startup added that the funding would allow it to accelerate the development and commercialization of its optical interconnect offering. “As AI scale-up domains extend across dozens of racks, optical interconnect becomes essential,” said Martin Lund, CEO of CScale. “At that scale, reliable, predictable communication is fundamental to system economics. Easier part replacement improves serviceability, not continuity. We’re designing the interconnect for continuity. Lasers will fail. Compute shouldn’t.” Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, added: "AI infrastructure is no longer just a compute problem. It is a systems problem. As scale-up systems move toward gigawatt-class deployments, interconnect bandwidth means nothing without system reliability. Every optical failure is a compute failure. At this scale, failures are not hypothetical—they are inevitable. CScale is designing reliable scale-up optics for next-generation AI factories, unlocking the full performance of optics without trade-offs.”

cards.body: Micron on Wednesday evening delivered a much better-than-expected quarter and indicated that its fiscal year 2027 will be another strong one as demand for its memory products continues to exceed supply. Revenue in the fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 3, rose 379% year-over-year to $54.23 billion, a beat versus the $51.07 billion consensus forecast, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increased 1,002% to $33.42, beating expectations of $31.61, LSEG data showed. MU YTD mountain Micron YTD Shares traded in a tight range in after-hours trading, but settled around the flat line after management finished its post-earnings conference call. The stock had a good September, rallying roughly 11%. For the year, Micron is up roughly 275%. However, it is down 12% from its record close of $,1213 on June 25. Bottom line It was a record-setting year for Micron as tight supply conditions and surging demand for memory in AI applications led to healthy increases in its average selling prices, resulting in soaring revenue, gross margins, and EPS. Remember, there are two main products in the memory market. There is NAND, which is storage memory, like a flash drive. There is also dynamic random access memory, or DRAM for short, which is considered working memory, like the RAM in your computer. There's also a specialized form of DRAM called HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, which is the key enabling technology for modern AI workloads. While AI accelerators do the math that underpins AI computing, they rely on HBM to store and feed them data. For AI to be deployed efficiently and at scale, systems require higher memory bandwidth and greater memory capacity. Due to the growing memory needs of AI systems, DRAM and NAND industry demand has significantly exceeded supply, and no one truly knows when the two will find a balance. As tight as memory and storage supply and demand conditions were in 2026, Micron expects conditions to be even tighter in calendar 2027 and 2028 because supply simply can't catch up to demand. Roughly 75% of Micron's expected output in 2027 is already spoken for, and customers are already speaking with the company on their allocations for 2028. "The structural gap between DRAM supply and demand growth rates is resulting in ongoing supply tightness, and cleanroom additions are required to augment node-transition supply growth and help narrow the gap," CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in the company's prepared remarks. Cleanroom additions refer to the physical expansion of manufacturing capacity by building and installing more equipment. Jim Cramer recently visited one of the company's massive semiconductor fabrication sites, or fabs as the industry calls them, which is under construction near headquarters in Boise, Idaho. cards.body: Amid escalating AI security incidents causing OpenAI to halt training and pause releases , Donald Trump continues to advocate for the AI industry to regulate itself as the best path to combat emerging risks when developing frontier AI. In an agreement Tuesday, two dozen tech firms voluntarily committed to implementing controls recommended by the White House, including undergoing independent safety audits that will test whether firms’ internal controls, monitoring, and detecting are actually working. Key focuses for external reviews included “risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity, chemical threats, and unintended actions by AI models.” Firms also agreed to regularly meet to discuss best practices and set common AI safety standards and benchmarks. Among signers were leaders like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Alphabet/Google’s Sundar Pichai. headlines.body: M.2 2230·2242·2280 등 다양한 폼팩터…소형 AMR부터 고성능 로봇 컨트롤러까지 대응 피지컬 인공지능(AI) 확산으로 로봇이 처리해야 할 센서와 영상 데이터가 급증하면서 고성능 프로세서뿐 아니라 이를 뒷받침하는 메모리와 스토리지의 중요성이 커지고 있다. 어드밴텍은 고속 DDR5 메모리와 소형 M.2 SSD를 중심으로 산업용 메모리·스토리지 제품군을 확대해 휴머노이드 로봇과 자율이동로봇(AMR), 산업용 로봇 시장 공략에 나선다. 어드밴텍은 SQ램 산업용 메모리와 SQ플래시 산업용 SSD를 기반으로 로봇 및 피지컬 AI 애플리케이션을 위한 메모리·스토리지 사업을 강화한다고 밝혔다. 최근 로봇은 카메라와 라이다(LiDAR), 관성측정장치(IMU) 등 여러 센서에서 수집되는 데이터를 실시간 처리하면서 AI 추론과 경로 계획, 객체 인식, 제어를 동시에 수행한다. 이에 따라 GPU·NPU 등 AI 프로세서의 성능과 함께 메모리 대역폭과 스토리지 입출력 속도, 안정성, 내구성이 시스템 성능을 좌우하는 요소로 부상하고 있다. 어드밴텍은 엔비디아, 인텔, AMD, 퀄컴 등과의 생태계를 기반으로 엣지 AI 컴퓨팅 플랫폼을 확대하는 동시에 자체 산업용 메모리·스토리지 제품을 연계하고 있다. AFE-A702와 ASR-A702 로봇 컨트롤러는 다중 카메라와 LiDAR, IMU 등의 센서 데이터를 처리하고 실시간 AI 추론을 수행하도록 설계됐다. 산업용 D램 제품군인 SQ램 SQR 시리즈는 DDR5 SODIMM을 비롯한 다양한 폼팩터로 구성된다. DDR5 4800·5600을 중심으로 6400과 7200까지 제품군을 확대하고 있다. DDR5 7200 기반 'SQR-SD5M 7200'과 'SQR-UD5M 7200'은 최대 64GB 용량과 7200MT/s 데이터 전송속도를 지원한다. DDR5 6400 제품과 비교하면 전송속도가 12.5% 높다. -25~95℃의 온도 범위를 지원해 고성능 엣지 컴퓨팅 환경에도 대응한다. 산업용 시스템에서 요구되는 장기 안정성에도 초점을 맞췄다. 주요 부품 구성을 고정하고 장기 공급을 지원하며 IC 세대 관리와 초기 고장 선별시험, 습도시험, 호환성 검증 등을 실시한다. 제한된 공간과 다양한 온도 조건에서 장시간 작동하는 로봇 시스템의 특성을 고려한 것이다. 스토리지 부문에서는 SQFlash SQF 시리즈를 앞세운다. M.2 2230·2242·2280 등 다양한 크기의 SSD와 PCIe Gen3·Gen4·Gen5 인터페이스 제품을 갖춰 로봇 시스템의 크기와 요구 성능에 따라 선택할 수 있도록 했다. 특히 M.2 2230은 공간 제약이 큰 소형 로봇과 엣지 디바이스에 적용하기 용이하다. 고성능 로봇 컨트롤러에는 M.2 2242·2280과 고속 PCIe 제품을 조합할 수 있다. SQF-C3M 730-D와 SQF-C4M 730-D는 PCIe Gen4 x4를 지원하며, SQF-C3M 740-F·C4M 740-F·C8M 740-F는 PCIe Gen5 x4 기반으로 최대 2~4TB 용량을 제공한다. SQF 740 시리즈는 PCIe Gen5 x4와 NVMe 2.0을 지원하며 최대 10GB/s의 순차 읽기 성능을 제공한다. DRAM-less 구조와 HMB(Host Memory Buffer)를 적용했으며 소비전력은 약 6W다. -25~85℃와 -40~85℃의 온도 옵션을 갖춰 AI와 산업용 엣지 컴퓨팅 환경에 대응한다. 어드밴텍은 국내 로봇 시장이 AI와 결합해 확대되면서 산업 현장의 고온·진동 등 다양한 조건에서 안정적으로 데이터를 처리하고 장기간 사용할 수 있는 산업용 메모리와 스토리지 수요도 증가할 것으로 보고 있다. 비키 수 어드밴텍 SQ램 제품 담당 매니저는 “피지컬 AI와 로봇 산업이 본격적인 상용화 단계로 진입하면서 AI 프로세서뿐만 아니라 이를 안정적으로 뒷받침할 수 있는 산업용 메모리와 스토리지의 중요성도 함께 높아지고 있다”며 “SQ램과 SQ플래시를 비롯한 산업용 메모리 및 스토리지 포트폴리오를 기반으로 고객의 로봇 시스템 설계와 다양한 엣지 AI 애플리케이션에 최적화된 솔루션을 제공할 것”이라고 말했다. 어드밴텍은 앞으로 DDR5 메모리와 PCIe/NVMe 기반 M.2 SSD 제품군을 지속 확대하고 로봇과 엣지 AI, 산업자동화 등 데이터 집약형 애플리케이션을 대상으로 산업용 메모리·스토리지 사업을 강화할 계획이다. 권상희 기자 shkwon@etnews.com
